extracted.intended_audience: computer-science and social-science researchers working on media bias detection (NLP practitioners, dataset creators, and interdisciplinary scholars)
extracted.subtask_description: A literature review and taxonomy for automated media bias detection methods, datasets, and human-centered research, aimed at guiding future computational and interdisciplinary work on media-bias identification and mitigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media Bias Taxonomy (five major categories)
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide media bias into five major categories: linguistic bias, cognitive bias, text-level context bias, reporting-level bias, and related concepts; provide subgroups for each category to precisely categorize sub-concepts related to media bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The taxonomy is presented as a crucial first step for establishing common ground in the domain. The authors iteratively revised definitions and structure and recommend future work critically re-examine and adapt the taxonomy to connect works across the area.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearly define the specific type/subtype of media bias under study
rubrics_metrics.description: Research must precisely state which subtype of media bias is being investigated (e.g., phrasing bias, framing bias, selection bias, partisan bias, cognitive bias).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to clearly define the type of media bias causes confusion when comparing studies. The review emphasizes that researchers often fail to define the bias type, which undermines comparability and conceptual clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annotator background reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Datasets should include information about annotators' backgrounds (demographics, political orientation, expertise) to contextualize subjective bias ratings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only two of 123 surveyed datasets included annotator background. The paper recommends standardized annotator background assessments because perception of bias depends on reader background and affects annotation quality and inter-annotator agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dataset size and coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Datasets should be adequately large and representative for the intended task; many existing datasets are small (only 21 of 123 have >30,000 annotations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The review notes small dataset sizes are common and suggests that the use of multiple datasets and larger-scale resources is promising for improving generalization and robustness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Task, label, and metadata clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Datasets and papers should report tasks, type of label (binary/ordinal/multi-label), availability, dataset statistics, and links for reproducibility and reuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors present a repository overview including publication summaries, sizes, availability, tasks, and label types as a starting point. Clear reporting facilitates comparison and reuse across studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple datasets and cross-domain / multi-task training
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine datasets and apply multi-task or cross-domain learning to leverage related resources and improve classification performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recent modeling techniques (e.g., extreme multi-task scaling, multi-task ordinal regression) enable joint use of related datasets; unsupervised/supervised pretraining across domains boosts results and helps when in-domain data are small.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate social-science insights and ensure rater representativeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporate human-centered research on bias perception into dataset design and modeling; ensure annotator samples are representative and account for cognitive/social factors that influence bias judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perception of bias depends on factors beyond content (reader background, social identity). Subjective bias ratings should be supplemented by objective bipartisan criteria (e.g., language-based measures). Integrating social-science insights can improve annotator agreement and annotation quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include social/contextual/network information where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Leverage social information (who shared an article, audience interactions, user-to-hashtag/mention graphs), metadata, and spreading behavior to capture contextual signals of bias and stance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Graph-based representations (node2vec, spectral graph transducer, GCNs) using social sharing information can significantly improve performance for some tasks (e.g., labeling political stance of pages/outlets). Transformer-based text methods alone cannot capture network properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select modeling methods appropriate to the bias subtype and application needs
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose between transformers, graph-based methods, traditional NLP, or hybrids based on the bias subtype, data modality (text vs. network), and requirements for explainability or performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transformers are currently the most frequently used and reliable for many detection tasks, but they have not been applied to all bias subtypes. Graph-based methods are better for network-structure analyses. Traditional approaches remain valuable as simpler, more explainable baselines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include explainable baselines and prioritize transparency when needed
rubrics_metrics.description: When transparency of classification decisions is critical (e.g., in deployed systems), include traditional NLP or non-transformer baselines and report explainability analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Traditional approaches and non-transformer deep models are simpler and more explainable; they often serve as baselines to compare to language-model-based methods and are preferable in contexts demanding interpretability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage large-scale pretraining and cross-domain transfer
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply unsupervised or supervised pretraining on massive corpora and cross-domain datasets to improve model performance and generalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transformer pretraining and cross-domain adaptation (facilitated by platforms like Hugging Face) can yield accurate results even with limited in-domain labeled data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze vector spaces and embedding properties to detect bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine the vector spaces of word embeddings and representation layers to identify and mitigate bias signals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vector-space analysis of embeddings is a promising complementary approach to improve classifiers and understand where bias manifests in representations (e.g., gender bias in layers of BERT). Causal mediation analysis and layer-wise inspection were cited as useful methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate bias at multiple levels of granularity
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess bias at different units (word/phrase, sentence, headline, article, reporting-level) because bias can manifest at varied granularities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies analyzing political bias and unfairness at different levels of granularity show that appropriate choice of granularity matters for detection and fairness analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standardize annotator questions and labeling protocols
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop standardized, domain-specific annotation questions and protocols to better capture bias perception and improve annotation consistency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The review suggests standardized questions within the domain can help integrate bias perception research into models, increasing inter-annotator agreement and improving annotation-based detection systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess interventions empirically and consider heterogeneous/backfire effects
rubrics_metrics.description: When designing and evaluating interventions (e.g., nudges, browser widgets, forewarning messages, training) to reduce biased perception, measure effect sizes, test for ideological heterogeneity, and watch for backfire effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical results show small average effects and possible backfiring (e.g., increased polarization or reduced credibility). Some interventions may be unequally effective across political groups; careful testing and tailored materials are necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge non-transparency and dynamics of algorithmic filtering
rubrics_metrics.description: Research examining social-media influences should account for the opaque, changing nature of algorithmic filtering and its limited transparency to users.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algorithmic filtering is not transparently disclosed and is in flux; this complicates assessment of social media's role in exposure and perceived bias and should be considered in studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide reproducible resources and repository metadata
rubrics_metrics.description: Publish dataset/table summaries, links, and publication summaries in an accessible repository to facilitate reuse and replication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors supply a detailed repository overview of publications, sizes, availability, tasks, label types, links, and summaries as a starting point, and recommend others do the same to support future work.
